## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Sāketajātaka* (Ja 68) is a canonical birth-story situated within the *Vissasavagga* (“Trust” section) of the Pali Jātaka collection [Anandajoti 2010; SuttaCentral]. The narrative opens with the verse phrase “The man thy mind rests on” and is assigned thematic titles such as “Faith at First Sight” [Anandajoti 2010] and “Friendship” [Humphreys 1956]. The story is set at the Añjanavana grove outside Sāketa, an important city of Kośala frequently visited by the Buddha and his disciples [Buswell & Lopez 2014; SuttaCentral].
According to the introductory story (*paccuppannavatthu*), as the Buddha entered the gate of Sāketa, an elderly local brahmin met him, embraced his feet, and affectionately reproached him as his son for neglecting his parents in their old age [SuttaCentral]. Taking the Buddha and the monastic assembly to his home, his wife similarly embraced the Buddha as her son and had her other children salute their elder brother [SuttaCentral]. After accepting their hospitality, the Buddha preached the “Sutta concerning old-age,” enabling both husband and wife to achieve the fruition of the Second Path (*sakadāgāmī*) [SuttaCentral]. To dispel the monks’ bewilderment over the couple’s display of parental familiarity, the Buddha revealed that the two had been his parents in many previous births [Anandajoti 2010].
